Hi! My name is Matthew Doty. I mostly work in industry, but from time to time I have been formalizing some of my largely independent research in Isabelle's Archive of Formal Proofs: https://isa-afp.org/authors/doty/

My research interests are in logic, computational complexity theory, probability theory, and finance.

I see CSLib doesn't have a completeness proof for propositional logic. When I've proven this in the past in Isabelle/HOL, I've used Zorn's lemma to prove strong completeness for the usual semantics using Maximally Consistent Sets. I'm curious whether this is an approach the CSLib folks want to take, or if they have another approach in mind.
cc @Thomas Waring who seems likely to have thoughts about the CSLib question

hi! i'll take a look at your past work when i have a chance, sounds interesting :)
i have completeness for (generalised) Heyting algebras, Kripke frames and (in the classical case) two-valued semantics in my branch — though somewhat messily at the moment. i haven't started PR-ing this as there are a couple of open propositional logic PRs already.
the Heyting case is fairly straightforward, and i derived the Kripke version (which i think is what you refer to as the "usual semantics") from it, so the Zorn's lemma argument is pushed into an application of (the dual of) docs#DistribLattice.prime_ideal_of_disjoint_filter_ideal (in an easily generalised form, see #38951).
let me know if you have further questions! progress is maybe a little review-bottlenecked at the moment, but there are plenty of interesting directions to develop this side of the library if you are interested in contributing :)) i mentioned some which i have (somewhat) thought about in this thread

Thomas Waring said:

i have completeness for (generalised) Heyting algebras, Kripke frames and (in the classical case) two-valued semantics in my branch — though somewhat messily at the moment.

So when I've worked on completeness, it's been via assignment expressions, roughly following Dirk van Dalen's *Logic and Structure*. This is similar to Kripke semantics without relations, although it predates Kripke.

I like how tight your proof is; doing this with assignment expressions requires more machinery in my experience.

A lot of logics extend propositional logic, and from time-to-time it's helpful when proving theorems to say "It follows from propositional logic that...". The way I did this in Isabelle/HOL was that I made a classical logic class, so we can haver a tactic that reduces the problem to classical logic assignment expression semantics, which are really well automated in Isabelle. Would this be something we'd want to try?

Another research interest of mine is probability logic. Is this something suited to CSLib?
